newsitem.title: JAPAN: MOF says following govt report on BOJ law reforms.
newsitem.headline: MOF says following govt report on BOJ law reforms.

text.p: Japanese Vice Finance Minister Tadashi Ogawa said on Thursday that discussions on reforming the law governing the Bank of Japan (BOJ) are following proposals laid out in a study group report.
"The talks are heading in the direction spelled out in the report by the study group (under Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto)," Ogawa told a news conference.
The study group submitted a report last year urging the government to change the law to enhance the bank's independence and transparency of its decision making.

Although the report did propose steps to curb some of the government's authority over the Bank of Japan, it fell short of suggesting that the BOJ be given independence equal to that of central banks in other major nations.
A MOF committee is currently finalising the bills to reform the BOJ laws, which will be sent to the current session of parliament.
Asked about the outlook of the negotiations with the United States over liquor tariffs and taxes, Ogawa said that the talks were still continuing and that he could not comment on the details.
Japan decided last year to raise taxes on domestic liquor and lower those for whiskey in order to comply with a World Trade Organisation (WTO) ruling.

MOF officials have said that the European Union, which made the complaint to the WTO along with United States and Canada, has basically agreed to the plan, while the United States and Canada have yet to reply.

Japan has offered to lower tariffs on bourbon whiskey as a substitute for U.S. complaints that the reduction in taxes, over a five-year period, would take too long. MOF is now waiting for Washington to reply, the officials said.
The Nihon Keizai Shimbun reported on Thursday that Japan has offered to scrap tariffs on bourbon whiskey, which now stand at 13.7 percent, by the fiscal year starting from April 2000.
Asked to comment on the foreign exchange market, Ogawa replied that his stance remained unchanged. He did not elaborate further.
